summary:
Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is an interactive web platform featuring a 2D exploration mini-game that brings the history of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars to life. Instead of presenting space history as static text, players actively explore lunar and Martian landscapes, discover real artifacts—such as the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Hasselblad cameras, and the Opportunity rover—and collect them to unlock concise, engaging stories about each mission.

This directly addresses the challenge by transforming NASA’s historical records and off-world hardware archives into an accessible, hands-on storytelling experience. By combining gameplay with verified mission history, our website turns passive readers into active explorers.

Preserving these stories is important because the equipment left behind on other worlds is not merely "space junk"—it represents decades of human ingenuity, sacrifice, and scientific breakthroughs. Making this legacy interactive inspires the next generation of explorers to appreciate how past missions paved the way for humanity's future in space.
details:
Space Museum: What Did We Leave Behind?

Humans have sent dozens of machines beyond Earth, and many have gone quiet. Rovers sit still on Mars, landers rest on the Moon, and Voyager keeps drifting between the stars. Space Museum asks: what were these machines built to do, and what did they teach us? It turns their stories into an adventure that school-age explorers can follow, touch and play.

 

What is Space Museum?

It is an interactive 3D museum for space enthusiasts and students. It starts with a cinematic story journey and opens into a full museum with an Equipment section, an Engineering Lab, and a Learning Zone. Users can use "Explore with Device" to pick a machine and try its real job in just a few minutes.

 

Features That Define the Experience:

A Story You Can Scroll

The opening journey moves from Earth to deep space, then Mars and the Moon. Each machine appears in 3D with a short mission goal (for example, Sojourner: "Show that a small robot car could drive on Mars and study its rocks"). Illustrated cards explain each part, like solar panels turning sunlight into electricity, cameras that took pictures and helped it steer, or rocket engines that slowed Surveyor 3 for a gentle landing. Skip-ahead, auto-play and sound controls let anyone move at their own pace.

 

Play a mission

Choose a machine and do its job. As Curiosity, you drive across Mars toward targets like Mudstone, the Old lake bed, Vein rock and Grey layer, with on-screen guidance showing distance to your next goal. Machine cards cover Curiosity, Perseverance, Opportunity, Spirit, Sojourner, Ingenuity, InSight and the Lunar Roving Vehicle.

 

Samples That Unlock Discoveries

Each sample you collect unlocks real science, such as evidence of water, the building blocks of life and food for microbes. Discovery pages let you tap numbered hotspots on a 3D model to learn what mudstone is, how it formed, how Curiosity collected it and why it matters. A Mars Science Journal tracks your entries and points.

 

Real NASA Images

Every discovery is paired with real NASA photographs, like the "John Klein" drill hole in Martian mudstone and the Yellowknife Bay formation. 3D models are clearly labeled as educational reconstructions based on NASA mission imagery.

 

Learning Made Fun

A friendly robot guide helps along the way, and an optional "Aliens, UFOs and space cows" mode adds humor, clearly marked as not part of the real history. Instead of a long article, the mini-game helps users learn engagingly.

 

Our Mission: Keeping Space History Alive:

These machines paved the way for human exploration, and their stories shouldn't fade when their signals do. Space Museum fuses storytelling, 3D visuals and playable missions with real NASA data so the next generation can ask: what will we build next?
